item.title: Main :: RE: sonic the hedgehog sega sg-1000/sc-3000 demake sprites i did
item.description:
Author: Maxim
Posted: Mon Nov 16, 2026 8:15 am (GMT 0)

Consider that SG-1000 sprites are 1-bit - you can only have more colours by overlaying them on top of each other, but then the sprite limit is also a limiting factor.

Then for the likes of Robotnik, you may instead use background tiles, but these can only have two colours per 8x1 sliver. Just converting things to the palette isn’t enough to fulfil the limitations of the hardware.

item.title: Development :: RE: [AI] Someone ran my homebrew through an LLM
item.description:
Author: bofner
Posted: Sun Nov 15, 2026 10:18 pm (GMT 0)

Kagesan wrote
A similar thing happened to me recently, when someone grabbed the ROM of my Bruce Lee remake, and ran it through Claude to have it slop-ported to Amiga and Atari ST. Last I checked, he was still asking for donations for all of "his" hard work on itch.io.


I'm really sorry about that. That's just vile. I can understand how someone might think they are "honoring" a game by porting it to another system using an LLM (though I do not see it that way) but once they're asking for money for someone else's work is where I stop being able to sympathize.

Maxim wrote
By publishing stuff online (as I have been doing for years) you have to accept that anyone can read it and now that means it can be used to train LLMs and also people can feed them to LLMs to generate nonsense. It’s unfortunate that this LLM part wasn’t even a thing when we published and there’s no way to stop them.


I considered changing my github to private for a moment. But if my code can help someone else learn an obscure skill that doesn't have as much documentation as modern languages do, then I guess its worth the risk of somenoe abusing my code to feed an LLM. Maybe "Open source upon request"? Idk. For now I'll keep it up

sverx wrote
Last June somebody had used an LLM to find 'security issues' in some of the tools in devkitSMS. They provided a PR with fixed code in their report.
I instead have preferred to not use the provided code and instead fixed the issues myself


That's the other thing too. If there's a bug in my code, and I'm explicitly not using AI to make my game, I don't really want someone else's agent to tell me about a bug. If another human tells me, that's fine, but if I'm essentially getting unsolicited AI assistance, at what point does my project stop being human-made?

item.title: Development :: RE: [AI] Someone ran my homebrew through an LLM
item.description:
Author: nothingsp
Posted: Sun Nov 15, 2026 4:43 pm (GMT 0)

chirinea wrote
I wonder if there shouldn't be a license that wouldn't allow people to feed the code to LLMs.

I'm sure that's something that will come out of this, but I suspect it will be ignored. "AI" pushers, from the model developers to the end users, operate on the assumption that they're entitled to just do whatever they want, and they'll go way past source-code license violations (look at how much violation of actual legally-enforceable copyrights they've already done.)

My long-term hope is that, once the money firehose funding this stuff dries up and it becomes economically impossible to operate at scale, this kind of thing goes away - but boy do I wish we could just skip straight to that part :/
